candidates.title: A Comprehensive Survey on Graph-Structured Small-Molecule Drug Discovery and Development with Deep Learning
candidates.abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery remains a cornerstone of modern therapeutics, yet traditional development pipelines are often limited by high costs, long timelines, and low success rates. Recent advances in graph-structured deep learning have significantly transformed the modeling of molecular structures, biological interactions, and pharmacological responses. By naturally representing molecules as graphs, these approaches provide an effective framework for capturing structural, geometric, and physicochemical information across multiple biological scales. In this survey, we present a comprehensive review of recent advances in graph-structured small-molecule drug discovery and development. To provide a unified perspective, we organize the literature into a four-layer framework covering data resources, representation learning, task formulation, and downstream applications. We first summarize the evolution of molecular representations from molecular sequences and topological graphs to geometric structures, molecular dynamics, and electronic field representations. We then introduce a unified task formulation covering six major tasks: molecular property prediction, drug-target interaction and affinity prediction, drug response and perturbation prediction, drug-drug interaction prediction, molecular generation, and molecular optimization. Building upon this framework, we review recent developments in graph neural networks, geometric learning, diffusion models, and foundation models. Finally, we summarize representative benchmark datasets and evaluation resources, and discuss several key challenges, such as out-of-distribution generalization and data scarcity, together with promising directions for future research.

candidates.title: Emerging Role of Artificial Intelligence in Natural Product-Based Drug Discovery
candidates.abstract: Background: Natural products remain an important source of therapeutic agents, but their discovery is constrained by chemical complexity, time-consuming isolation, difficult structure elucidation, and high attrition rates. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, and generative AI, offers computational approaches to address these challenges. Method: This narrative review examines peer-reviewed, English-language literature published between 2021 and 2026, retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The selected literature was analyzed using thematic qualitative synthesis to identify AI applications, reported contributions, and persistent limitations across the natural product discovery pipeline. Problem Identification: Despite growing interest in AI-assisted drug discovery, the extent to which current methods address the limitations of conventional approaches remains uncertain. Key concerns include data quality, model reliability, interpretability, and the need for experimental validation. Results: AI applications cover target identification, biosynthetic gene cluster mining, virtual screening, structure elucidation, network pharmacology, generative molecular design, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) prediction. These methods can help prioritize candidate compounds and predict potential biological activities. However, data scarcity and bias, inconsistent evaluation practices, limited interpretability, and insufficient experimental validation remain significant barriers. Explainable AI, multi-omics integration, and self-driving laboratories represent promising developments, although their practical contributions require further validation. Conclusion: AI can support and accelerate selected stages of natural product-based drug discovery but cannot replace experimental testing or the expertise of natural product chemists and pharmacologists.

candidates.title: A closed-loop framework for perovskite precursor additive discovery
candidates.abstract: Efficient discovery of precursor additives is essential for improving the performance of perovskite solar cells, yet the large chemical space makes conventional trial-and-error screening inefficient. Here we show that LEAP (LLM-driven Exploration via Active Learning for Perovskites), a closed-loop framework combining a domain-specialized language model with active learning, prioritizes perovskite precursor additives under low-data conditions. The model extracts mechanism-relevant knowledge from the literature and converts it into interpretable molecular descriptors for uncertainty-aware Bayesian optimization. On an evaluation drawn from unseen literature, the specialized model provides more mechanism-consistent answers than the tested general-purpose models. In an expert-guided proof-of-concept study, two later-round additives increase average device power conversion efficiencies to 20.13% and 20.87%, compared with 19.25% for the control, and the best device reaches 21.32%. Because only a limited number of candidates are tested prospectively, these results provide preliminary evidence that literature-grounded molecular representations, Bayesian optimization, and expert assessment can support additive discovery for perovskite solar cells. Discovering effective perovskite precursor additives is challenging due to the vast chemical space. Here, the authors present a closed-loop active-learning framework that leverages literature knowledge to accelerate perovskite precursor additive discovery, achieving solar cell efficiencies up to 21.32%.

candidates.title: From structure prediction to ligand–target recognition: expanding the reach of AlphaFold in natural product research
candidates.abstract: Natural products constitute a structurally diverse reservoir of bioactive molecules and remain an important source of lead compounds for drug discovery. However, the limited availability of structural information on pharmacological targets and biomolecular interactions continues to hinder mechanism elucidation and structure-guided optimization, particularly for complex natural products such as bioactive peptides, proteinaceous natural products, and natural molecular glues. Recent advances in AlphaFold have transformed structural biology by enabling high-confidence prediction of protein structures and biomolecular complexes, providing unprecedented opportunities for structure-guided natural product research. Beyond conventional structure-based virtual screening, emerging co-folding strategies have demonstrated considerable potential for improving early enrichment in natural product screening and for elucidating the binding mechanisms of complex natural products with their targets. This review summarizes recent advances in AlphaFold-assisted natural product research, including target structure prediction, hit and lead discovery, co-folding-enabled interaction analysis, mechanistic investigation of peptide- and protein-derived natural products, and the emerging potential of AlphaFold for natural molecular glue discovery. We further discuss current limitations and future directions in structure prediction and interaction modeling. Overall, AlphaFold is reshaping natural product research from lead discovery to mechanistic characterization, with particular promise for advancing macromolecular natural products and molecular glue-mediated therapeutics.

candidates.title: Techno-economic optimization of a heat-pipe microreactor, part II: Multi-objective optimization analysis
candidates.abstract: Heat-pipe microreactors (HPMRs) are compact and transportable nuclear power systems exhibiting inherent safety, well-suited for deployment in remote regions where access is limited and reliance on costly fossil fuels is prevalent. In prior work, we developed a design optimization framework that incorporates techno-economic considerations through surrogate modeling and reinforcement learning (RL)-based optimization, focusing solely on minimizing the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) by using a bottom-up cost estimation approach. In this study, we extend that framework to a multi-objective optimization that uses the Pareto Envelope Augmented with Reinforcement Learning (PEARL) algorithm. The objectives include minimizing both the rod-integrated peaking factor ( F Δ h ) and LCOE—subject to safety and operational constraints. We evaluate three cost scenarios: (1) a high-cost axial and drum reflectors, (2) a low-cost axial reflector, and (3) low-cost axial and drum reflectors. Our findings indicate that reducing the solid moderator radius, pin pitch, and drum coating angle—all while increasing the fuel height—effectively lowers F Δ h . Across all three scenarios, four key strategies consistently emerged for optimizing LCOE: (1) minimizing the axial reflector contribution when costly, (2) reducing control drum reliance, (3) substituting expensive tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) fuel with axial reflector material priced at the level of graphite, and (4) maximizing fuel burnup. While PEARL demonstrates promise in navigating trade-offs across diverse design scenarios, discrepancies between surrogate model predictions and full-order simulations can lead to infeasibility in some cases, particularly for fuel lifetime and shutdown margin. Therefore, this study should be understood as a surrogate-guided trade-off exploration study rather than an effort to identify exact Pareto-optimal solutions. Further improvements are anticipated through constraint relaxation and surrogate development, constituting an ongoing area of investigation.

candidates.title: Lighting‐Consistent Object Transfer Across Radiance Fields
candidates.abstract: Abstract 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is widely used to capture and render real scenes. Compositing objects from one capture into another has applications in many domains, such as VFX, architecture and interior design, or marketing. However, extracting an object from a source scene and naively pasting it into a target scene will fail to produce realistic results due to the different lighting conditions between the two scenes. To address this problem, we introduce a diffusion model that harmonizes naively composited images with inconsistent lighting. The model is trained with a heterogeneous dataset of image pairs (inconsistent composite input, consistent output), combining synthetic, generated, and real data. Our complete 3D solution allows a user to extract an object from the source scene and composite it into the target scene. From this, the (inconsistent) views of the target scene with the composite object are rendered. Our diffusion model harmonizes each one of these views, which are finally consolidated in a 3DGS representation with a post‐optimization step. Our method provides visually compelling results, making object transfer between 3DGS easy to use and significantly improving quality compared to previous methods.

candidates.title: OneMall: One Architecture, More Scenarios — End-to-End Generative Recommender Family for E-commerce
candidates.abstract: In the wave of generative recommendation, we present OneMall, an end-to-end generative recommendation framework tailored for e-commerce services at Kuaishou. Our OneMall systematically unifies the e-commerce's multiple item distribution scenarios, such as Product-card, short-video and live-streaming. Specifically, it comprises three key components, aligning the entire model training pipeline to the LLM's pre-training/post-training: (1)E-commerce Semantic Tokenizer : we provide a tokenizer solution that captures both real-world semantics and business-specific item relations across different scenarios; (2)Transformer-based Architecture : we largely utilize Transformer as our model backbone, e.g., employing Query-Former for long sequence compression, Cross-Attention for multi-behavior sequence fusion, and Sparse MoE for scalable auto-regressive generation; (3)Reinforcement Learning Pipeline: we further connect retrieval and ranking models via RL, enabling the ranking model to serve as a reward signal for end-to-end policy retrieval model optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneMall achieves consistent improvements across all e-commerce scenarios: +14.7% GMV in Product-Card, +10.3% GMV in Short-Video, and +4.9% GMV in Live-Streaming. OneMall has been deployed, serving over 400 million daily active users at Kuaishou.

candidates.title: Extending AIMNet2 to Macrocyclic Peptides through Data-Efficient Continual Training
candidates.abstract: Abstract Macrocyclic peptides are among the most promising therapeutic modalities, yet no general-purpose machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) has been systematically benchmarked for their conformational analysis. We show that on the MPCONF196 macrocyclic benchmark, the four-model AIMNet2 ensemble outperforms MACE-OFF23(S), despite macrocycles being entirely absent from its training data. A single AIMNet2 model is 3- to 5-fold faster and needs 5- to 63-fold less GPU memory than the MACE-OFF23 models at their default float64-precision. The four-model ensemble is about as fast as MACE-OFF23 but retains a 3- to 32-fold memory advantage even against MACE-OFF23 in float32. The larger MACE-OFF23(M) and MACE-OFF23(L) models remain more accurate. To narrow this gap, we introduce a continual training protocol that requires new quantum-chemical labels for fewer than 25,000 domain-specific conformers (<0.13% of the training corpus) while preserving conformational-energy accuracy on nonmacrocyclic molecules. On a sequence-disjoint holdout of unseen CREMP macrocyclic peptides, the resulting model, AIMNet2-macro, reduces conformational energy RMSE by 25 to 27% and DFT force RMSE by 20% (25% on backbone atoms) and improves lowest-energy conformer recovery relative to the original AIMNet2. It retains the conformational-energy accuracy of the original model on the nonmacrocyclic drug-like molecules of CONFORGE and also improves accuracy on the structurally distinct macrocycles of MPCONF196, although this smaller improvement is not statistically significant. Among the ten training strategies compared, only continual training on the combined corpus (AIMNet2-macro) achieves this improvement without degrading small-molecule accuracy. AIMNet2-macro is therefore the best balanced, though not the most accurate, of the models tested. As an independent case study, AIMNet2-macro reproduces DFT conformational energies of six cyclosporine A conformers with an RMSE of 0.78 kcal mol–1 and the correct rank ordering, the lowest error among the MLIPs and semiempirical methods evaluated on this system. The continual training strategy has been adopted in the AIMNet2 (2025) release, which unifies small-molecule, macrocyclic, and intermolecular-interaction treatment in a single production potential.

candidates.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
candidates.abstract: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.

candidates.title: An aggregation-prone region in talin controls talin self-interactions and regulates integrin adhesion complex dynamics
candidates.abstract: Abstract The tight regulation of the integrin family of extracellular matrix (ECM) receptors is essential for the coordination of most cellular processes. Talin regulates integrin function by binding to the cytoplasmic tail of the integrin beta subunit. Two integrin-binding sites (IBS) in talin have been reported, one in the talin head domain (IBS1), and a second in the C-terminal rod region of talin (IBS2), mapped to the R11-R12 domains. Whilst the structural details of integrin binding to IBS1 are well understood, IBS2’s mode of binding integrin is less clear, and the biochemical details of this site have been elusive. Here we report that talin R11 contains a cryptic high affinity talin-binding site. We show that mechanical unfolding of R11 exposes an Aggregation Prone Region (APR) in Helix50 that oligomerizes with other talin R11s. Our data support a model whereby the process of mechanically unfolding one R11, exposes and maintains the APR in a high affinity conformation that drives unfolding of other R11 domains and oligomerisation. Atomic Force Microscopy confirms that the APR region alone forms micron long amyloid-like fibres, via a beta-sheet amyloid arrangement which can be abolished using a canonical “gatekeeper” point mutation, V2078K, that prevents APR interactions. Introducing this gatekeeper mutant in talin eliminates recruitment of talin IBS2 to integrin adhesion sites. The APR region in talin overlaps with a vinculin-binding site in Helix50, and we show a novel role for vinculin as a mechano-chaperone for talin, able to resolve the talin large species by binding to the VBS in Helix50. In light of this new information, we propose that the ability of R11-R12 to target to integrin adhesion complexes and enhance integrin activation can be better explained by a model where functional aggregation of talin serves to recruit and activate more talin molecules at the adhesion site leading to enhanced integrin activation. Whilst further work is required to fully exclude integrin binding to R11 we suggest that the name IBS2 might be a misnomer and propose the name Aggregation Prone Region 1 (APR1) for this talin oligomerisation motif.

candidates.title: Enterovirus 2C Protein Drug Design, Assay Development, and Drug Resistance Studies.
candidates.abstract: In this Account, we describe our efforts to establish enteroviral 2C as a tractable target for antiviral drug discovery by integrating medicinal chemistry, molecular pharmacology, resistance profiling, structural modeling, and assay development. Rather than relying solely on conventional phenotypic high-throughput screening, our initial studies focused on the rational optimization of reported 2C inhibitors identified from a drug-repurposing campaign. This strategy led to quinoline-based antivirals with substantially improved potency and selectivity against enterovirus D68 (EV-D68), providing early medicinal chemistry insights into ligand recognition by enteroviral 2C and supporting the feasibility of chemically targeting this protein. Building on these findings, we subsequently developed pyrazolopyridine-based inhibitors, which evolved into one of the most potent classes of enteroviral 2C inhibitors reported to date. Mechanistic studies combining differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF), serial viral passage, reverse genetics, and molecular modeling supported direct engagement of a conserved allosteric pocket corresponding to the previously defined (S)-fluoxetine binding site. Structure-guided optimization led to Jun6504, a rationally designed 2C inhibitor with improved metabolic stability, favorable pharmacokinetic properties, and robust in vivo efficacy in a neonatal mouse model of EV-D68-induced paralysis. Collectively, these studies provided strong pharmacological validation of 2C as a therapeutically actionable antiviral target. In parallel, we recognized that the absence of direct, scalable biochemical assays was a major impediment to 2C-targeted antiviral discovery. To address this bottleneck, we developed a fluorescence polarization-based binding assay that monitors ligand engagement of the conserved allosteric pocket in enteroviral 2C proteins. Using Jun14157, a fluorescent probe derived from the pyrazolopyridine inhibitor series, this platform enabled direct, quantitative, and high-throughput characterization of ligand-2C interactions across EV-D68, EV-A71, and CVB3. Coupling this assay with structure-based virtual screening further enabled the identification of new allosteric inhibitor scaffolds and established a generalizable discovery platform for enteroviral 2C inhibitors. Together, these studies define an integrated framework for enteroviral 2C antiviral discovery, spanning hit-to-lead optimization, mechanism of action studies, resistance mapping, pharmacological validation, and assay innovation. Continued advances in inhibitor-bound structural elucidation, broad-spectrum inhibitor design, and next-generation therapeutic strategies should further accelerate the development of clinically useful antivirals targeting enteroviral 2C proteins.

candidates.title: Generative design for additive manufacturing through data-free optimization-derived neural weight subspaces
candidates.abstract: Abstract Generative design (GD) enables exploration of diverse shape variants that exhibit trade-offs among competing design objectives related to part manufacturability and performance, offering a transformational approach towards automated part design for advanced additive manufacturing (AM). However, existing GD methods often derive design diversity either from large datasets of existing designs or through topological modifications, limiting their applicability to data-scarce engineering problems, particularly for complex parts where manufacturability and preservation of topology and geometric features are critical. In this work, we present a training-free generative design framework that leverages the optimisation trajectory of a single neural field-based shape optimisation to represent and explore neural field variants within a low-dimensional neural weight subspace. Our design space exploration is realised through a Langevin diffusion-inspired stochastic process with energy-conditioned guidance, enabling the generation of constraint-satisfying shape variants that provide distinct objective trade-offs. The framework generalises across geometrically and topologically diverse complex parts, including freeform geometries with intricate surface features and non-trivial topology. We validate the method through simulations and physical additive manufacturing experiments, demonstrating support-free 3D printing of the generated shape variants and establishing a data-free route towards manufacturability-aware generative design for complex parts.

candidates.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Dual-Target Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery Under Strict Homology Constraints
candidates.abstract: The worldwide escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe challenge to modern public health, necessitating novel classes of therapeutic agents. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent highly promising alternatives to small-molecule antibiotics due to their co-evolutionary resilience and rapid membrane disruption dynamics. However, translating computational AMP leads into clinical drug candidates remains bottlenecked by off-target cytotoxicity, predominantly hemolytic activity against mammalian erythrocytes. Although pretrained foundational protein language models (PLMs) have rapidly advanced molecular property prediction, current architectures frequently isolate antibacterial potency and cytotoxicity into disconnected single-task pipelines or succumb to catastrophic performance drops under strict homology-controlled evaluations. Recently, the Quantitative Mapping of Antimicrobial Peptides (QMAP) benchmark proposed that frozen PLM embeddings show weak linearly accessible features for hemolytic activity (HC50) resulting in poor rank correlation ({rho} < 0.25) on out-of-distribution sequence splits. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end multi-task parameter-efficient transfer learning framework designed to simultaneously optimize antibacterial potency and minimize mammalian cytotoxicity without sequence leakage. Built upon ESM-2 (150M), our architecture incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into self-attention projections, fine-tuning approx 0.70% of model weights. To restore gradient interference originating from disparate membrane lysis mechanisms, we implement an adaptive multi-task loss guided by Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. Evaluated across predefined QMAP benchmark splits enforcing a 60% maximal sequence identity threshold, our joint architecture remarkably outperforms conventional linear probes, tree-based regressors, and frozen foundational models. The framework achieves an E. coli potency rank correlation of {rho} = 0.6132 (r = 0.6816) and successfully elevates hemolytic toxicity correlation to {rho} = 0.5374 (r = 0.5541). To establish real world utility, we deploy the optimized joint network to screen a curated in silico library of 749 de-novo designed peptides, successfully isolating selective cationic-amphipathic candidates possessing Therapeutic Indices (TI = HC50/MIC) up to 144.03 while effectively deprioritizing broadly lytic motifs (TI < 2.0). These findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient adaptation unlocks fine-grained bioactive structural semantics in foundational PLMs, providing an accurate, scalable framework for therapeutic peptide engineering.

candidates.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Generative Science of Food Formulation
candidates.abstract: Food formulation requires balancing taste, nutrition, sustainability, and cost. Traditionally, new foods have emerged through empirical experimentation, expert intuition, and iterative refinement. Now, artificial intelligence (AI) offers the opportunity to accelerate this process. Yet despite rapid advances across food science, most AI applications remain isolated prediction and optimization tasks rather than parts of a broader scientific approach. Here we integrate these emerging technologies into a unified framework—the generative science of food formulation—in which digital food representations enable AI to predict, discover, generate, organize, simulate, and optimize. We illustrate this approach through sustainability and nutrition, where generative AI transforms environmental and nutritional metrics from post hoc evaluation criteria into explicit design objectives. Finally, we identify the data, models, benchmarks, and automation that will establish computational food design as a rigorous scientific discipline. Together, these advances have the potential to transform food formulation from an empirical discipline into a generative science.

candidates.title: Procedural Adversarial Learning
candidates.abstract: For many computer vision tasks, neural networks can be trained to produce a low average error, yet they still fail on seemingly simple scenes. Reducing these failures requires first finding them, but they may not be in a fixed dataset. We study procedural adversarial learning (PAL), a framework of minimax training and adversarial evaluation which searches the input space of a procedural generator for difficult instances. The procedural generator is an interpretable program mapping a low-dimensional vector of control parameters (e.g. layout, lighting, pose) to a rendered image and its label. We introduce the Simple-PAT algorithm, which uses zeroth-order optimization in the procedural generator's parameter space to propose adversarial training samples that are generated on demand. We also create PAL-Dojo, a collection of efficient procedural generators for surface normal estimation, image segmentation, and human pose estimation. Against a cross-model black-box adversary with 50M aggregate queries, Simple-PAT reduces worst-case error by a geometric mean of 3.15x compared to standard training and 2.63x compared to the strongest robust training baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/princeton-vl/procedural-adversarial-learning.

candidates.title: Nonparametric modelling of continuous-time Markov chains with scalable exact and approximate gradients
candidates.abstract: Abstract Inferring the infinitesimal rates of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) is a central challenge in many scientific domains. This task is hindered by 3 factors: quadratic growth in the number of rates as the CTMC state space expands, strong dependencies among rates, and incomplete information for many transitions. We introduce a new Bayesian framework that flexibly models CTMC rates by incorporating covariates through Gaussian processes. This approach improves inference by integrating new information and deepens our understanding of CTMC stochastic behaviour by shedding light on potential external drivers. Unlike previous approaches limited to linear covariate effects, our method captures complex nonlinear relationships, enabling fuller use of covariate information and more accurate characterization of their influence. For efficient posterior inference, we employ Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. To avoid the prohibitive cost of repeated matrix-exponential derivatives under existing approaches, we develop 2 scalable strategies for exact and approximate gradient computation. Given N observations and K CTMC states, these strategies reduce the cost from O(NK3), with a substantial constant, to O(K3+NK2), with cheaper constants. We demonstrate the method in Bayesian phylogenetic and phylogeographic inference, showing strong performance on synthetic and real datasets and empirical quadratic scaling in K, even when N<K.

candidates.title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors
candidates.abstract: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.

candidates.title: Fast Solution Methods for the Classical 0–1 Knapsack Problem
candidates.abstract: The classical 0--1 knapsack problem is among the simplest integer programs to state and among the most instructive problems for understanding why algorithm selection must follow instance structure. An input contains items with positive integer weights and profits, and the task is to choose a maximum-profit subset whose total weight does not exceed a capacity. The problem is weakly NP-hard, yet many large instances are solved quickly because exact algorithms exploit moderate numeric parameters, strong linear relaxations, dominance relations, or a small set of uncertain variables near the fractional break item. This review develops a theory-guided account of the principal fast solution methods for the classical problem. It proves the correctness and complexity of weight-indexed and profit-indexed dynamic programming, explains sparse Pareto-frontier implementations and reconstruction, derives the fractional-knapsack upper bound used by branch-and-bound methods, and establishes the correctness of meet-in-the-middle search. It then presents the core concept that underlies influential practical solvers and gives a detailed proof of the standard profit-scaling fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. Modern advances based on structured min-plus convolution are placed within this classical landscape rather than treated as isolated results. The central conclusion is that there is no universally fastest knapsack algorithm. Small item counts favor meet-in-the-middle search, moderate capacities or total profits favor dynamic programming, favorable density structure favors core-based exact methods, and very large numeric coefficients favor approximation. A final decision framework translates these theoretical distinctions into an implementable solver-selection policy while identifying open questions concerning adaptivity, certified switching among methods, memory efficiency, and realistic hard-instance generation.

candidates.title: FoXSight: Facilitating Computational Hit Identification in Crystallographic Fragment Screening Experiments
candidates.abstract: X-ray crystallographic fragment screening reveals how small molecules bind to proteins, providing important starting points for drug design. Identifying these weak binding events remains difficult when electron density signals are noisy, partially occupied or obscured by solvent, and campaigns may comprise thousands of datasets. Here, we present FoXSight, a computational method for hit identification in crystallographic compound screening. FoXSight applies Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) filtering to multi-reference subtraction maps to detect recurring, target-specific density features associated with bound ligands. Its output maps remain visually interpretable and support subsequent ligand modeling. We evaluated FoXSight on in-house and public datasets spanning seven protein targets, comparing its maps with PanDDA where suitable comparison data were available. FoXSight was successfully used as the primary hit identification tool in a challenging crystallographic fragment screening campaign for human Cathepsin L, where the output of established methods was impractical to inspect systematically.

candidates.title: A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation
candidates.abstract: Real-time phase estimation on stimulus-aligned transient EEG is critical for closed-loop neuromodulation systems targeting the theta-band, yet most real-time phase estimation methods have been developed and validated on resting-state, high-fidelity signals in the alpha band. Recent work has pursued deep learning architectures, while individualized classical bandpass filter tuning remains underexplored. This study characterizes the spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering and demonstrates the performance gains achieved through individualized tuning. We present a Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model evaluated on EEG recorded during peripheral vibrotactile stimulation of the left median nerve (theta, N=20 healthy subjects) and on resting-state recordings from the Max Planck Institute's LEMON dataset (alpha, N=20 healthy subjects). BOB was benchmarked against the Deep Dual-Branch Complex Neural Network (DBCNN), EEG Phase Prediction Network (EPN), Phastimate, and Phase Estimation with Autoregressive Padding (PEAP) under matched testing conditions: channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation time points, and an offline reference phase obtained through zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform. Under these testing conditions, BOB achieved matched or better performance than these models at a fraction of the calibration time.

candidates.title: A novel ferro-aging-related gene signature for prognosis and targeted drug prediction in cervical cancer
candidates.abstract: Abstract Objective Cervical cancer (CESC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women. Recent studies have identified ferro-aging as a genuine biological pathway in primates, representing an iron-dependent metabolic process. However, cellular ageing and the decline in overall physiological function play a crucial role in tumour progression. Based on this, we have established a prognostic model related to ferro-aging and evaluated its predictive and diagnostic value in cervical cancer. Methods We integrated data from the The Cancer Genomics Atlas (TCGA), the Gene Expression Online Resource (GEO) and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Following the identification of ferro-aging-related gene (FARGs) based on the literature, we constructed a prognostic model using machine learning algorithms and analysed model features via Shapley-based interpretability (SHAP) analysis. The Scissor algorithm was employed to evaluate cell populations associated with high- and low-risk groups. Studies on intercellular communication and spatial transcriptomics revealed the process of tumour microenvironment remodelling. Finally, potential therapeutic compounds were identified through AI-assisted virtual screening and molecular docking. Results A total of eight FAR model genes were ultimately identified: DUOX1, E2F1, IL1B, KEAP1, MAP3K14, SLAMF8, TFRC and TNFAIP3 . This study constructed and validated a novel risk profile model comprising these eight ferro-aging-related genes; this model demonstrated moderate prognostic discriminatory power in both internal and external cohorts, with the tumour microenvironment in the high-risk group exhibiting an immunosuppressive state. Using single-cell RNA sequencing to assess cellular heterogeneity, macrophages, epithelial cells and CD8 + T cells were identified as key factors in CESC progression. Pseudotime analysis was performed to visualize the expression levels of FARGs along the pseudotime axis and explore how FARGs participate in the dynamic process of EndMT. Spatial transcriptomics was employed to map the distribution and expression of FARGs within epithelial cells in the tumour microenvironment. Intercellular communication intensity was increased in the low-risk group, with epithelial cells in this group signalling to macrophages via the APP-CD74 pathway. Drug screening indicated that BRD-A56371469 is likely to bind to DUOX1. Conclusions The FARG signature is a robust independent prognostic indicator for CESC. The integrated pipeline offers insights into ferro-aging biology and suggests novel therapeutic candidates.

candidates.title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
candidates.abstract: Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

candidates.title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI
candidates.abstract: Current generative AI alignment relies on a myopic paradigm that prioritizes immediate conversational satisfaction. By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift toward long-horizon alignment that accounts for how AI reshapes human experience over time. To this end, we map the tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs of AI use across four facets of human well-being to reveal outcomes that current reward models fail to capture. Ultimately, we advocate for moving beyond simple preference optimization toward alignment strategies that actively foster long-term human well-being by navigating these complex temporal scales.

candidates.title: Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
candidates.abstract: Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. To model developing visuomotor circuits and behavior, we investigated whether a single compact generative encoding could produce functional recurrent controllers across such changes. Building on the HyperNEAT algorithm, we represented this program as a compositional pattern-producing network that received developmental time as an input to generate age-specific connectivity. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. We tested this approach using two geometrically distinct developmental substrates and two visuomotor tasks: optomotor responses and phototaxis. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.

candidates.title: Nano-Bioadhesives for Gastrointestinal Hemostasis and Healing: Integrating Artificial Intelligence for Precision Design and Application.
candidates.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding and mucosal injury remain clinically challenging because most bioadhesives lose performance under acidic, enzymatic, and peristaltic conditions. Nanotechnology has advanced adhesive design by enhancing mechanical integrity, degradation control, and antimicrobial activity; however, translating these gains into consistently favorable clinical outcomes is still difficult. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a route to accelerate and derisk development. Here, we identify predictive, multiobjective materials design as the AI domain most critical for GI nanobioadhesives because adhesion, hemostasis, degradation, biosafety, and healing must be optimized simultaneously. Predictive modeling, molecular simulations, and high-throughput experimentation enable rational control of adhesion strength, degradation kinetics, and biocompatibility, while machine-learning models expedite the discovery of optimal polymeric nanoparticle formulations. Emerging strategies such as digital twins and closed-loop optimization further support patient-specific and adaptive adhesive systems. By integrating AI-guided design with nanotechnology platforms, next-generation GI bioadhesives could unify rapid hemostasis, antimicrobial protection, and regenerative functions, thereby improving reliability and clinical translation. This review outlines the synergy between AI and nanotechnology and highlights priorities for advancing GI adhesive therapies from bench to bedside.

candidates.title: Library size and structure, not synthetic labels, explain apparent benchmark--experiment discrepancies in antibody machine learning
candidates.abstract: Abstract Synthetic benchmarks are widely used to develop machine-learning methods for antibody--antigen binding, but the conditions under which their conclusions transfer to measured data have been examined narrowly. Typical synthetic and measured datasets differ not only in whether labels are simulated, but also in library size, library structure, alignability and measurement noise. We show that these covarying factors, not the labels, account for the apparent differences. Holding a lattice oracle fixed and rebuilding its library as 6{,}000 mutational variants of one parent, we compared it against measured affinities for four therapeutic targets and a third-party campaign of 119{,}828 measurements. Before matching, the regimes disagreed about the search advantage, the preferred representation and architecture, and learnability decomposition. After matching, three of the four disagreements disappeared and the fourth proved unmeasurable: the search advantage fell from 1{,}620-fold to single digits, 3.3-fold against 3.0-fold measured, and a protein language model overtook one-hot encoding on the matched lattice. Surviving effects include a threefold search advantage, a Spearman cost of 0.105 from measurement noise, and an 8.1-fold overstatement by random splits. Synthetic benchmarks are faithful proxies when conditions are matched; the problem lies in uncontrolled comparison.

candidates.title: SoK: The Security-Safety Continuum of Multimodal Foundation Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) integrate diverse data modalities to support complex and wide-ranging tasks. However, this integration also introduces distinct safety and security challenges. In this paper, we unify the concepts of safety and security in the context of MFMs by identifying critical threats that arise from both model behavior and system-level interactions. We propose a taxonomy grounded in information theory, evaluating risks through the concepts of channel capacity, signal, noise, and bandwidth. This perspective provides a principled way to analyze how information flows through MFMs and how vulnerabilities can emerge across modalities. Building on this foundation, we introduce a deterministic minimax formulation to analyze defense mechanisms and to study a structural asymmetry of defense in multimodal systems. Our analysis indicates that model-centric defenses, which primarily operate by suppressing noise or enhancing signal, tend to exhibit diminishing effectiveness against increasingly adaptive attacks. In contrast, system-level safeguards that constrain authorized information flow and agent behavior impose stronger limits on adversarial impact by reducing effective bandwidth. To operationalize this insight, our framework maps attacks and defenses onto information-theoretic axes, effectively organizing and reducing the defense search space. Using a proposed Defense Coverage Index (DCI) to evaluate 15 representative defenses, we observe that system-level bandwidth constraints provide stronger and more consistent protection across attack classes than brittle model-level mechanisms. Finally, we formalize an MFM ``self-destruction threshold'' that specifies when termination should be triggered, offering a concrete activation rule for circuit-breaker safeguards in multimodal systems.

candidates.title: FoxO1 and HNF1α cooperatively remodel nucleosome architecture and mechanical stability to activate transcription
candidates.abstract: How different transcription factors (TFs) cooperate to bind nucleosomal DNA targets remains unclear. Cryo-EM and force spectroscopy show that the pioneer factor FoxO1 binds superhelical location (SHL) +2 of nucleosomes assembled on the human IGFBP1 promoter, enhances distal DNA unwrapping, destabilizes the histone core, and reduces nucleosome mechanical stability. TF HNF1α binds SHL +5/+7 as a dimer, induces extensive DNA unwrapping without perturbing the histone core, and reshapes nucleosome disassembly dynamics. FoxO1 enhances HNF1α recruitment, and together they stabilize the nucleosome during its mechanically-induced disassembly trajectories. In-cell nucleosome footprinting on active promoters shows that FoxO1 binding enhances unwrapped nucleosomes and subnucleosomes presence, while HNF1α increases stabilized and breathing nucleosomes and reduces the subnucleosome population. Combined, they display an intermediate nucleosome phenotype. Our data leads to a model where FoxO1 destabilizes the nucleosome and enhances HNF1α recruitment, and together they remodel nucleosome architecture both in vitro and in native chromatin.

candidates.title: Beyond LLM Serving: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Workloads for Embodied AI System Design
candidates.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate multimodal observations into low-level robot actions. During robot operation, each control period sets an inference deadline, and overruns leave the robot acting on stale observations, reducing task success. Meeting this deadline motivates on-device or nearby edge execution, where a single robot requires batch-1 inference outside the design point of LLM serving systems. Although VLA architectures combine familiar vision-language, autoregressive, and diffusion-style components, their runtime behavior in this batch-1 control setting remains uncharacterized. We characterize four representative VLA models on an edge GPU server and two onboard SoCs, using single-inference profiling and 43,200 closed-loop episodes. Action tensor dimensionality determines whether a stage is memory- or compute-bound, platform balance can shift that bottleneck, and GPU frequency scaling yields a platform-dependent energy-latency sweet spot. In closed-loop operation, overlapping inference with action execution creates an accuracy-speed-energy tradeoff, and no configuration is Pareto-dominant across deployment SLOs. These results guide joint design of VLA model architectures, hardware, and runtime policies.

candidates.title: Molecular basis of Cyclin B1-CDK1 recruitment by MAD1
candidates.abstract: The interaction between Cyclin B1-CDK1 and MAD1 recruits kinase activity to the nuclear pore complex and kinetochore corona to sustain spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) signaling. Here, we characterize a short linear motif (SLiM) within MAD1 that mediates its interaction with Cyclin B1. This SLiM peptide is specific for B-type cyclins and lacks the canonical "RxL" cyclin-binding consensus sequence, suggesting a distinct mode of cyclin recognition. Using a combination of deep mutational scanning, structural analysis by cryogenic electron microscopy, and binding affinity measurements, we define the molecular basis of the Cyclin B1-MAD1 interaction. These approaches reveal that a short MAD1 peptide binds as an -helix to the RxL-binding hydrophobic patch of Cyclin B1. The interaction employs hydrophobic contacts that overlap with those used by canonical RxL motifs, but is distinguished by additional contacts and sequence features that confer preferential recognition by B-type cyclins while excluding other cyclin types. We also show that the MAD1 motif is sufficient to confer B-type cyclin-specific substrate phosphorylation in mitotic cells. Together, these findings reveal a non-canonical, B-type cyclin-specific helical binding mode that ensures selective Cyclin B1-CDK1 recruitment at two critical stages of SAC signaling, and suggest potential strategies for selective therapeutic targeting of this interaction.
